newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: DUTCH A2000 EYES GROWTH AFTER PHONE LICENCE WIN.
newsitem.headline: DUTCH A2000 EYES GROWTH AFTER PHONE LICENCE WIN.

text.p: Cable television operator A2000, a joint venture between Philips Electronics NV unit UPC and US West International said it was looking to snap up more subscribers as it geared up to offer telephony services.

"They (acquisitions) have to fit the philosophy which is to operate in those areas where you have a high density and that's big cities. If you have adjacent areas that's fine...but we wouldn't start with a small city," A2000 chief executive Hans Wolfert said in an interview.
A2000 says it aims to be the first cable TV firm to offer telephony to consumers after winning a licence last month.
"Whenever there's an opening we make a bid. We don't try to be hostile. We don't think there's any point in being more aggressive and going outside bidding structures," he said.

A2000 has its eyes on some of the cable operations of Casema after Koninklijke PTT Nederland agreed to cut its Casema stake to a minority in order for Casema to qualify for a regional infrastructure licence.

"It's an interesting process that's happening with Casema. If we can get into that discussion we will, although we're not interested in all the properties of Casema," said Wolfert, adding the firm operated around the Netherlands.

A2000 has around 525,000 subscribers in the Amsterdam region and the nearby town of Hilversum. "We're going to offer the new services to about one third of our customers before the end of 1997, then within two years everyone will be able to buy the services from us," Wolfert said.

He declined to give details of market research indicating likely demand but said the models provided by the roll-out of cable companies following telecommunications deregulation in Britain were positive, although the markets were very different.
"This PTT is different to BT. It doesn't have big holes allowing competition, they're geared up to face competition."
A2000 will offer consumers telephony from July 1, when its licence comes into force, but will also be targeting small to medium-sized businesses.

"Because of our cable network we go closer to the potential user with fibre optic backbones. The overlay of fibre, which gives you in telecoms terms wider availability of network, is much closer and for businesses that's interesting," he said.

Consumers would be attracted by the options of hooking up to the internet and receiving special telecoms and video packages through one operator. "It's hard to imagine for most people that you can get that from just one plug," said Wolfert.
The company has said it would invest around 300 million guilders in the next few years to prepare the cable network for telephone and internet services.

"We're here to stay and it's a long term investment. We're not talking money payback in two or three years we're talking about five to eight years in terms of breaking even. From there on, it should be a healthy investment and profit," he said. -- Keiron Henderson, Amsterdam Newsroom +31 20 504 5000
